segments.text: - Welcome back. We turn now to my interview
with Byron Donalds, the Republican candidate for governor.
We covered a wide array of topics,
but I wanted to discuss education with him
because I don't believe it has received enough attention.
We recorded this interview on Wednesday,
and then on Thursday,
the Miami Herald published a story
about his wife, Erika Donalds, and her business dealings
with charter school companies in Florida.
That story appears to contradict some
of the statements Byron Donalds
made to me during our interview.
We'll get into that in a few moments.
But on the broader question of education policy,
critics of Donalds believe his goal
is ultimately to do away with traditional public schools,
so I started by asking him that very question.
Would we be better off if education was privatized?
In other words, like that if we
eliminated traditional public schools
and just turned to a system where private companies
and others were responsible for educating our children,
the public would still be paying for it
through the vouchers and the rest of it.
I guess I'm wondering, do you believe
that traditional public schools
are a hindrance at this point?
- No, I don't go that far.
And let's be clear, traditional public schools,
as we've known them in our country,
has been a staple in a fabric of America
the last hundred years.
I think if you believe in choice like I do,
I believe putting parents in a position
to make those decisions,
giving them purchasing power
in order to make those decisions
on behalf of their children,
that's not to eliminate traditional public schools.
It's letting parents decide
where they think the best environment is for their child.
I think having that broad choice
for parents to make that decision,
whether it's the local public school
or whether it's the local charter school now,
because we have a lot of charter schools
that's been operating in our state for quite some time,
or the local private school, again,
operating in our state in many communities
for quite some time.
It's about parents making those decisions.
That's what I believe.
- But it seems as if there is a perception
that what you will ultimately lead the state to
is an elimination of the traditional public school system.
That by putting more money and resources
into diverting children to charter schools
or private schools through vouchers,
that it chokes off public schools,
the traditional public schools.
Address the notion that a Donalds administration
would lead us towards the end
of public education as we know it.
- Jim, I think you're listening to my critics
more than anything else.
That's something that I've never said.
It's never come out of my mouth.
I've never even insinuated.
Do I believe parents should have the choice
to choose where their children go to school?
Absolutely.
That is what I believe.
I've been consistent on that, really, for a decade,
even when I served in the state House.
But I've also said that traditional public schools
are not going anywhere.
The school districts have the infrastructure.
They have most of the teachers.
They're gonna be embedded in every community in our state.
I think what we're seeing is we're having this fight
where either you believe in choice
or you believe in traditional public schools
and there's no middle ground.
I actually don't believe in that.
If anything, Florida is really creating
that middle ground right now.
We have half a million kids in the state of Florida
who are in a school of choice,
but even within the public school system,
most of the kids within the public school system
are now having choice
within the traditional district system.
It's about empowering parents about where they wanna go.
Look, I'm not here to eliminate public schools.
As a matter of fact, part of my proposals
is to actually take off the categoricals
on school funding from the state level
to give traditional districts more flexibility.
Whether they wanna negotiate with teachers
or come up with programming for students,
we wanna give those superintendents
and those principals more flexibility.
I think where we're going in Florida
is having a choice environment that parents choose,
which is the environment today.
From a state, we wanna make sure parents are aware
of what are the outcomes?
How are kids reading?
How are kids doing math?
Are kids being able to write at a high level in high school?
What's the ACT score?
What's the SAT score?
Or like my LaunchPad initiative states,
do these children have an opportunity
to go into the working world
and get an apprenticeship or an internship?
That's education with me as governor.
It's gonna be about parental choice,
not an elimination of traditional public schools.
- Okay.
Here's where the Herald story about Erika Donalds
will now come into play.
As I mentioned earlier, we taped this interview
with Byron Donalds on Wednesday.
On Thursday, the Herald published this lengthy investigation
under the headline, "How Byron and Erika Donalds' wealth
hinges on millions in state education dollars."
It shows how Erika Donalds' companies
are making millions managing charter schools
that are funded with state tax dollars.
Now, keep that in mind as you listen
to this next part of my interview with Byron Donalds.
What role do you envision your wife playing
as it relates to education?
Because she has been in this space.
This is an area that she's done well in,
in terms of management of charter schools and the rest.
We talked about this before.
Is it still the plan that she will have
no business involvement with charter schools
in the state of Florida?
- She doesn't have business involvement today
and she's not gonna have that going forward.
- Will she be one of your advisors on this?
What role will she play? - I mean, come on, Jim.
She's my wife.
Of course she's gonna have advice.
I mean, any husband takes advice from their wife.
Let's be very clear.
But if you're talking about who's gonna be making
the decisions when it comes to education,
that will be me.
I wanna be clear with you.
There's only one governor at a time.
And when it comes to education policy
or any other policy governing the state of Florida,
those are decisions that I will be making
about how we execute the mission
that we receive from the legislature.
- Okay, again, listen to my question and his answer.
Is it still the plan that she will have
no business involvement with charter schools
in the state of Florida?
- She doesn't have business involvement today
and she's not gonna have that going forward.
- I asked the campaign to reconcile what he told me
with what the Herald reported,
and this is what they said.
"Congressman Donalds was referring
to Optima Management Services' former contracts
to provide charter-school management services
to independent brick-and-mortar schools.
Those schools have transitioned to self-management,
those contracts have ended,
and there are no plans to resume that work."
But the campaign does acknowledge that Erika will continue
to work with virtual online charter schools in Florida,
and they do not dispute the facts of the Herald story.
Now, we will have their complete statement
at cbsmiami.com for you to see,
but let's also now return to my interview
with Byron Donalds.
You know, David Jolly will say
that you've spent upwards of $100 million
and have not been able to close the deal,
that the more money you spend
and the more people get to know you,
the less they are inclined (Byron chuckles)
to vote for you, but I do wanna ask the question,
why do you think having spent $100 million,
you haven't been able to close the deal and widen the gap?
- Well, actually, I think that's the wrong way
to look at it.
Look, first of all, this is a new governor's race.
It's an open governor's race.
I think if David Jolly was running against Ron DeSantis,
he'd lose by 12 points
because everybody knows who Ron DeSantis is.
He's had eight years of governance in our state.
The voters of Florida are beginning to know me.
And actually, and I was on the governor's campaign
eight years ago against Andrew Gillum,
and it was tough sledding then.
I think anytime you have a new person
trying to take the role of being a state's governor,
there's a lot of defining that you have to do,
explaining yourself to the electorate.
A lot of voters who are out there undecided...
Well, it's actually shrinking by the day now,
but undecided voters who are now coming
to this election saying,
"Okay, do I wanna continue the same vision
that we've seen from Governor DeSantis,
or do we wanna go a new way similar to what's happening
in Virginia or New York or New Jersey?"
And I think the voters of Florida
are gonna be very clear on November 3rd.
They don't want a up north state.
They don't want blue governance.
They want us to have
the same consistent conservative governance
that's made Florida the best state in America.
- You're now using in your campaign commercials
very strongly that you are endorsed by Ron DeSantis.
You had a complicated relationship with the governor,
that is pretty clear.
After your endorsement of President Trump,
I think you've even acknowledged that things
sort of grew somewhat tense.
Does it feel strange at all to you to now turn more
to the fact that Ron DeSantis is supporting you
than President Trump is supporting you?
- No, I don't think so.
I mean, look, everybody in Florida knows
that we have the endorsement of President Trump.
You even acknowledge we've spent a lot of time
during the primary making that point known
to the voters in our state,
but now as we come down the stretch,
it's important to let the voters know
where Governor DeSantis sides in this election,
and that's very clear as well.
At the end of it all,
it's about Florida and the people of our state.
We've been focused as we've crisscrossed every community
about talking about the issues that matter to them,
from insurance to housing to transportation,
how we manage growth, water quality,
the future of electricity in our state.
These are the issues that we've been talking about,
and that's what matters
to the people of Florida. - Yeah, but given
the contentious relationship you've had with the governor,
it must have hit you a little bit that you now,
as part of your closing message, have to say-
- Nah. - "It's Ron DeSantis
is supporting me, so therefore you should vote for me
because I have his seal of approval."
How do you think he perceives that?
- No, I don't think that's an issue at all.
I think, look, were there issues back in a couple years ago?
Yeah, of course, but that's life.
You get over it.
It's about where do you want Florida to go next.
- Have you asked the governor- - And I think if you-
- To come campaign with you?
- And I think if you look at what the governor talks about,
his view of where Florida should go,
it's very clear what side of the fence he's on in this race,
and so we communicate that to the voters.
- Have you asked him to come campaign with you?
- The governor and I have talked about several events.
We did one about a month ago or so in Tampa,
and that was a really good event,
but we've been crisscrossing the same...
I wanna be very straight with you on this.
I think the way you campaign for a governor
or for any other position,
you can have even a key surrogate like the governor come in,
and that's wonderful.
But at the end of it all, it's about you going to campaign.
You gotta go see the voters.
And Jim, you know this.
We've been in every community
in Florida repeatedly for months.
The reason why you do that
is because you're asking the voters to choose you
to be the next governor.
- So, one of those communities
that you've been putting some emphasis on recently
seems to be Black voters.
When we talked six months ago,
I think it was, in the interview,
you somewhat wanted to downplay
the racial aspects of this race,
the historic nature of this race,
you being potentially the first Black governor
in the state of Florida.
It seems, and correct me if I'm wrong,
you seem to be leaning into that just a little bit more
in these final few weeks,
in part making a pitch to Black voters to consider you.
- Well, actually, the pitch we've made
to Black voters is not about history.
And I'm well aware.
Reporters have been talking about it.
People ask me about it.
We've still been focused on those same issues.
Whether I'm in Overtown or Little Haiti
or I'm up in the Panhandle,
what the people of Florida mostly care about,
lowering the costs in this state.
They want it to be affordable for seniors,
for working families.
Young families are trying to buy homes in our state.
We wanna make sure we have a growing and stable economy
so they have high-paying jobs
while we take care of the governmental problems that exist
so that we can lower those costs,
and that's the stuff that we've been talking about.
Does history come up?
Yeah, it comes up, but it's really about the issues
and the vision for the future of Florida.
- The issue of race is one
I also recently discussed with David Jolly,
and I wanted Donalds to react to one of the things
that Jolly specifically said about him.
I wanna play for you what Jolly said to me last month,
and then you will hear Donalds' response.
- It is Republican leaders and candidates like Byron Donalds
who have attacked voting rights for Black
and Brown communities who have defunded initiatives
that have economically empowered communities.
It is Byron Donalds and his colleagues
that defund public education,
making sure in some communities that you have one type
of education opportunities and, in another, you don't.
It is Byron Donalds that has accepted health disparities,
the outcome disparities for healthcare
in different communities based on color.
There's a greater disparity today, Jim,
between black and white America
than the day Martin Luther King
gave his "I Have a Dream" speech,
and I know that and Byron Donalds doesn't.
- David Jolly is a fraud.
He's just saying things to try to find ways
to draw more wedges in the Black community.
I find it to be very unfortunate
that that's the way he will go.
Considering the fact that he didn't wanna get
into labels in this campaign.
If you notice what he's been doing for the last month,
there's been a lot of labels that come from him.
Let me be very clear.
My agenda, whether it's Black Floridians or any Floridian,
is about them being able to flourish.
When we talk about multiple pathways
for success in education,
it's because whether it's a Black kid in North Miami
or a White kid in Levy County,
we want them both to have multiple pathways
to be successful in life.
That's actually looking forward about their ability
to build a great dream in Florida.
When we talk about permitting reform,
something I've been doing consistently for two years,
we talk about that to lower the cost of construction,
thereby making housing more affordable.
How does that even deal with creating
some sort of racial barrier?
That doesn't even make any sense.
Quite frankly, it's insulting that you would have somebody
who just became a Democrat literally like 10 months ago,
all of a sudden now lecture me
about what policies stand for or one way or the other.
If you look at the agenda
that we have put forward- - Well, what he's suggesting
is that you are bad for African Americans.
- Yeah, and he has to say that
because he's lying to African Americans and he's fraudulent.
This is a guy who, 10 years ago,
agreed with me on some of these issues,
but now he's switched his positions
only because he switched his party.
